events.title: Chromium-based Microsoft Edge released
events.summary: Microsoft shipped the Chromium-based Edge on January 15, 2020 — abandoning EdgeHTML for the same engine that powers Chrome.
events.about: The new Edge traded engine independence for compatibility: sites built for Chrome worked out of the box, and Microsoft contributed back to Chromium. It ended the era of three competing engine families (Gecko, WebKit/Blink, EdgeHTML) and consolidated the web platform around Blink for most users.

narrative.whyChosen: Microsoft joining Chromium was a watershed moment in browser engine consolidation.
narrative.whyImportant: It acknowledged developer reality — Chrome compatibility mattered more than a proprietary engine.
narrative.problemSolved: EdgeHTML could not keep pace with Chrome's site compatibility and release cadence.

events.title: Python 2 reaches end of life
events.summary: The Python Software Foundation ended support for Python 2 on January 1, 2020 — closing twenty years of the 2.x line and forcing the ecosystem onto Python 3.
events.about: After January 1, 2020, no bug fixes or security patches came from the core team for Python 2 — even for critical vulnerabilities. Enterprises running legacy Django apps, scientific code, and ops scripts had to port, freeze, or pay vendors for extended support. The migration had been announced since 2008 and extended once; this was the hard deadline.

narrative.whyChosen: Python 2's sunset was one of the largest coordinated language migrations in open-source history.
narrative.whyImportant: It ended ambiguity about which Python to teach, ship, and depend on — Python 3 became the only supported line.
narrative.problemSolved: Maintaining two incompatible Python dialects split library authors and slowed language evolution.
